[DOC-01 p.1 - Key finding: the ventilation paradox] In quiescent microgravity, flames over thin PMMA and cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric weakened and
self-extinguished at oxygen levels that support burning on Earth. The combustion products build up
around the flame and the oxygen supply is limited by slow diffusion. Adding a weak forced flow of
roughly 5-10 cm/s - comparable to normal spacecraft cabin ventilation - brought in fresh oxygen
without the large convective heat losses of buoyant flow on Earth. In this low-speed range the
limiting oxygen index (LOI) fell **below** both the quiescent microgravity value and the normal-gravity
value. In practice, a cabin ventilation fan can keep alive a flame that would otherwise go out.

[DOC-05 p.2 - Findings] - **Peak flammability at intermediate gravity.** Thin fabrics in parabolic-flight Lunar profiles had
  LOI values 0.5-1.5 percentage points below their 1g value. The effect was strongest in the Artemis
  34 % / 56.5 kPa atmosphere.
- **Mars (0.38g)** behaved more like 1g, with a buoyant velocity of about 15-19 cm/s. Its flammability
  was similar to or slightly above 1g.
- **Adding forced ventilation** to partial-gravity buoyancy can push the effective velocity past the
  flammability peak. This depends on direction and magnitude, so habitat ventilation design changes
  fire behaviour.

[DOC-01 p.3 - Implications for spacecraft fire safety] 1. **Shut down ventilation immediately.** Cutting cabin ventilation as soon as a fire is detected
   removes the oxygen supply that low-speed flow provides. Without that flow, a weak microgravity
   flame goes back to the starved, quiescent regime. This supports the existing ISS practice of
   shutting off fans as the first fire response.
2. **Earth-based material tests are not always conservative.** The normal-gravity upward
   flammability test (NASA-STD-6001B Test 1) is usually considered conservative. However, thin
   materials in low-speed concurrent flow can burn at oxygen levels slightly below their 1g limit.
   The margin between cabin O2 and a material's LOI should account for this.
3. **Watch for smouldering and re-ignition.** After extinction, samples sometimes smouldered. When
   the flow was restored, a hot ember could re-ignite.

[DOC-02 p.2 - Partial-gravity and 1g comparison] A subset of runs repeated the exploration atmospheres in parabolic-flight Lunar (0.16g) and Mars
(0.38g) profiles and in a ground laboratory (1g). At 0.16g, weak buoyant flow acts like a gentle
ventilation velocity of about 10-12 cm/s, close to the most flammable flow regime. See DOC-05.

[DOC-05 p.3 - Summary table] | Gravity | Buoyant velocity (56.5 kPa) | Flammability vs 1g |
|---|---|---|
| 0g, quiescent | 0 cm/s | lower (starved) |
| 0g, 5-10 cm/s ventilation | 5-10 cm/s | higher |
| 0.16g Lunar | ~9 cm/s | higher (peak) |
| 0.38g Mars | ~15 cm/s | similar / slightly higher |
| 1g | ~22 cm/s | reference |
